# **Chapter I: Introduction**

Drones require many systems to work together cohesively, to complete a mission we need multiple datastreams and commands to ensure that the drone completes its mission successfully.The Robot Operating System (ROS) is a set of software libraries and tools for building robot applications. From drivers and state-of-the-art algorithms to powerful developer tools.This paper contains the development of Aerobase’s ROS2 drone system. From installation to integration, this paper will dive into how Aerobase utilizes its assets.

## **2.1 Installing Python and Pip**

Setting up a Python virtual environment (venv) is a great way to isolate your project dependencies, especially when working with ROS 2 or any Python-based project. Python virtual environments help decouple and isolate Python installs and associated pip packages. This allows end-users to install and manage their own set of packages that are independent of those provided by the system or used by other projects.

Open up your terminal and follow the steps below:  
**Step 1: Install Python**  
sudo apt update  
sudo apt install python3 python3-pip

Checking if installed  
python3 \--version  
pip3 \--version  
**Step 2: Install venv (Virtual Environment)**  
	sudo apt install python3-venv  
**Step 3: Make your directory and cd into it, then create venv**  
	mkdir my\_project  
cd my\_project

python3 \-m venv venv   
**Step 4: Source and Activate the venv**  
	source venv/bin/activate  
		venv\\Scripts\\activate  
	**Step 5: Install all your pip libraries**  
		pip install \--upgrade pip  
		pip install numpy rclpy  
		pip install dronekit  
		pip install open-cv  
		pip list  
	**Step 6: Deactivate**  
		deactivate  
	**Step 7: Reactivate venv**  
		source venv/bin/activate

## **3.1 Setup and Installation**

### **3.1.1 Install the required libraries**

**![][image10]**  
Install rclpy with : source /opt/ros/\<ros2-jazzy\>/setup.bash  
Install opencv with : pip install opencv-python  
pip install opencv-python-headless   
Install numpy with : pip install numpy  
Install ros2 messages : sudo apt install ros-\<ros2-jazzy\>-std-msgs  
\#The time library is not necessary, it is only used if you need to display fps

### **3.1.2 Making ROS2 Packages for OpenCV**

1. Open the terminal and type : cd \~/ros2\_ws/src  
2. To make a package type : ros2 pkg create \--build-type ament\_python \--license Apache-2.0 \<package\_name\>. **Replace \<package\_name\> with your preferred package name.**  
3. After creating a package, to create a talker (publisher) node and listener (subscriber) node, go to \~/build/\<package\_name\>/build/lib/\<package\_name\> and make **two** new python files.

## **3.2 Publisher Node Brief Explanation**

The publisher node should be able capture the camera frames, detect objects, calculate its offset to the center of the screen, then process the frames and publish both offset and the processed image to the subscriber node.

### **3.2.1 Object Detection**

One way to detect objects is masking. After masking, get its contours then calculate its center by using moments. Then calculate the offset by calculating the center of the object and the center of the frame. Publish the offset.

### **3.2.2 Image processing**

Draw the contours of the objects into each frame. After calculating the offset, draw the offset into each frame. Then publish the processed frame.

## **3.3 Subscriber Node Brief Explanation**

The subscriber node should be able to get the offset data and the processed frame. After getting both, print the offset on the terminal and show the processed frame.  
Source:[https://docs.ros.org/en/jazzy/Tutorials/Beginner-Client-Libraries/Writing-A-Simple-Py-Publisher-And-Subscriber.html\#write-the-publisher-node](https://docs.ros.org/en/jazzy/Tutorials/Beginner-Client-Libraries/Writing-A-Simple-Py-Publisher-And-Subscriber.html#write-the-publisher-node)

## **TROUBLESHOOTING**

1. ### **Image not displaying**

   1.1 use cv\_bridge  
   1.1.1 Download cv\_bridge by typing ‘pip install cv\_bridge’ on terminal  
   1.1.2 Import cv\_bridge to your code as CvBridge to both **talker** and **subscriber** code  
   1.1.3 Create a variable to publish the camera data with its message type as ‘Image’ and its topic ‘image’  
   1.1.4 Create a variable to call the CvBridge function  
   1.1.5 Convert opencv type to ros2 imagemessage type by using ‘cv2\_to\_imgmsg’ and set its encoding parameter to ‘bgr8’  
   1.1.6 Publish the converted data  
   1.1.7 On the subscriber code, make a callback function called ‘camera\_callback’  
   1.1.8 Create a variable to subscribe to the published camera data by setting its message type as ‘image’, its topic as ‘image’ and, callback to the ‘camera\_callback’ function  
   1.1.9 On the ‘camera\_callback’ function, create a variable to convert the subscribed data back to opencv type by using ‘imgmsg\_to\_cv2’ and set desired\_encoding to ‘bgr8’  
   1.1.10 Show the converted data using ‘imshow’

2. ### **Subscriber node doesn’t get the offset / processed image**

   If this happens, make sure the topic that you set on the publisher node is the same as the subscriber node.

## **3.- Troubleshooting ROS2**

There are many problems when trying to execute your ros2 code, we have experienced many with the python modules. First we start with some things you have to do before executing your code.

1. Make sure you are in the right workspace, don’t forget the layout of your workspace.  
2. Make sure your system is able to apt update and also be able to colcon build your workspace.  
3. Source your ros2 setup with, source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash  
4. Source your installations as well with, source install/setup.bash (the 2nd step should have the same effect).  
5. Try to run your code again, ros2 run \<your\_package\> \<your\_node\>.  
   

**‘No Module Found’ Problem Fixed**

1. See where is your current dronekit file is located, python3.12 \-c "import dronekit; print(dronekit.\_\_file\_\_)".  
2. Make sure the file location is inside your ros2 workspace/install/…/lib/python3.12/site-packages.  
   Example:  
   /home/maul/ros2\_ws/install/drone\_kit\_arm/lib/python3.12/site-packages/dronekit/\_\_init\_\_.py.Now make sure you can locate the dronekit folder and **\_\_init\_\_.py** file.  
3. Optionally you can add the python path by running it on your terminal.  
   export PYTHONPATH=$PYTHONPATH:\<your path to the site packages\>  
   Example:  
   export PYTHONPATH=$PYTHONPATH:/home/maul/ros2\_ws/install/drone\_kit\_arm/lib/python3.12/site-packages  
4. Source your bashrc, source \~/.bashrc  
   

**‘module 'collections' has no attribute 'MutableMapping' Problem Fixed**

1. Find your dronekit folder and \_\_init\_\_.py file  
2. Edit the \_\_init\_\_.py file, find MutableMapping and add abc like this,  
   class Parameters(collections.abc.MutableMapping, HasObservers):  
3. If you cannot use VsCode then nano into the \_\_init\_\_.py file, like this  
   nano /home/maul/ros2\_ws/install/drone\_kit\_arm/lib/python3.12/site-packages/dronekit/\_\_init\_\_.py  
4. Finally run your ros2 code again.

 


# **Chapter V: Gazebo**

## **4.1 Getting Started with Gazebo**

Gazebo has a lot of integration with ROS2.  
see: [https://gazebosim.org/docs/latest/ros2\_overview/](https://gazebosim.org/docs/latest/ros2_overview/)  
**IMPORTANT NOTE: WE ARE USING GZ SIM NOT CLASSIC GAZEBO11**  
Let’s start describing the different types of integrations that you can achieve between Gazebo and ROS.

* Use ROS to launch Gazebo: ROS prescribes a specific way to launch all the pieces needed in your system. There’s a dedicated [launch mechanism](https://docs.ros.org/en/rolling/Tutorials/Intermediate/Launch/Creating-Launch-Files.html) to orchestrate the launch of all your components and many tooling around it. Gazebo can be launched in this way.  
* Use ROS to interact with Gazebo topics via the [ros\_gz bridge](https://github.com/gazebosim/ros_gz): Once Gazebo is up and running, it’s very common to communicate with the simulation. A common way to perform this communication is via topics. Gazebo has its own middleware, Gazebo Transport, that exposes a set of topics and services quite similar to ROS. The ros\_gz bridge allows you to create a bridge between Gazebo and your ROS system that translates between Gazebo Transport and ROS 2 as needed.  
* Use ROS to spawn a Gazebo model: Gazebo worlds can include models that are loaded at startup. However, sometimes you need to spawn models at runtime. This task can be performed using ROS 2\.

**Composition**

If you inspect the parameters of the launch files mentioned in the next tutorials, you’ll notice that we have included in most cases a parameter named use\_composition. When that parameter is set to True, the associated ROS node will be included within a ROS container. When this happens all the nodes live within the same process and can leverage interprocess communication.

Our recommendation is to always set the use\_composition parameter to True. That way, the communication between Gazebo and the bridge will be intraprocess. If your ROS nodes are also written as composable nodes, make sure that they are launched with the container\_node\_name parameter matching the container name including Gazebo and the bridge.

You can learn more about ROS composition in [this tutorial](https://docs.ros.org/en/galactic/Tutorials/Intermediate/Composition.html).

**Optional**

After installing Gazebo, you can also launch Gazebo Sim from a terminal.

Option 1: Launch Gazebo by running:

gz sim shapes.sdf  \# Fortress and Citadel use "ign gazebo" instead of "gz sim"

This command will launch both the Sim server and Sim GUI with a world that contains three simple shapes.

Option 2: Add the \-v 4 command line argument to generate error, warning, informational, and debugging messages on the console.

gz sim shapes.sdf \-v 4  \# Fortress and Citadel use "ign gazebo" instead of "gz sim"

Option 3: Gazebo Sim can also be run headless, i.e. without the GUI, by using the \-s (server only) flag.

gz sim \-s shapes.sdf \-v 4  \# Fortress and Citadel use "ign gazebo" instead of "gz sim"

Similarly, the GUI can be run independently using the \-g (gui only) flag. On start, the GUI will attempt to connect to a server instance. If a server is not available, then you will see just a blank screen until a server instance is started.

Don’t forget to assign your domain ID for ros:

Domain ID 0: This is the default domain ID. If all nodes use ROS\_DOMAIN\_ID=0, they can all communicate with each other.  
Domain ID 1 (or other numbers): If you set the domain ID to a different number, such as 1, then only nodes that share that domain ID (1) will be able to communicate.

## **4.5 Making a Gazebo Model / Map**

A **Gazebo model** consists of 3D meshes, textures, and physics properties that define how an object behaves. A **Gazebo map** represents a larger simulated environment, including terrain, walls, and objects.

To create a model or map in Gazebo, ensure you have the necessary tools:

* **Gazebo** (installed with ROS or standalone)  
* **SDF (Simulation Description Format)** or **URDF (Unified Robot Description Format)**  
* **Blender/MeshLab** (optional for custom 3D models)

### **4.5.1 Importing a Gazebo Model Directly from Gazebo Sim**

1. Launch Gazebo

gz sim

2. In Gazebo, go to the **Insert** tab (on the left panel).

3. Browse the available models from the **Resource Spawner.**

4. Click and drag the desired model into the simulation environment.

### **4.5.2 Importing a Model from Other Sources**

You can download models from external sources (e.g., Gazebo Model Database) and place them in the \~/.gazebo/models/ directory to use them in your simulation.

### **4.5.3 Importing a Model from Blender**

1. Make a model in Blender

2. After you are done with the model, export the model as .obj format

3. In Gazebo, go to the Entity Tree tab and press \+, and press “meshes”

4. Find the model on your directory  
   

Visually, the model is done. But we are making a drone, the drone has to have moving parts such as the propellers, lidars, etc.

### **4.5.5 Importing a Model from Blender**

A **Gazebo map** is a simulated environment that defines the terrain, objects, and structures in a Gazebo world. It allows robots to navigate, interact, and perform tasks in a virtual space.

Key Components of a Gazebo Map

* **World File (.world)**: Defines the environment using XML-based SDF format.  
* **Terrain & Objects**: Includes ground, buildings, obstacles, and lighting.  
* **Physics & Sensors**: Simulates real-world physics and sensor interactions.

### **4.5.6 Add the Model to Gazebo**

Move the `.obj` file and textures to your Gazebo model directory:  
bash  
CopyEdit  
`mkdir -p ~/.gazebo/models/custom_map/meshes`

`mv your_model.obj ~/.gazebo/models/custom_map/meshes/`

`mv your_texture.png ~/.gazebo/models/custom_map/materials/textures/`

1. 

Create a **model.config** file in `~/.gazebo/models/custom_map/`:  
xml  
CopyEdit  
`<model>`

  `<name>CustomMap</name>`

  `<version>1.0</version>`

  `<sdf>model.sdf</sdf>`

`</model>`

2. 

---

### **3\. Define the Model in SDF**

Create a `model.sdf` file in the same directory (`~/.gazebo/models/custom_map/`):

xml

CopyEdit

`<sdf version="1.6">`

  `<model name="custom_map">`

    `<static>true</static>`

    `<link name="map_link">`

      `<visual name="visual">`

        `<geometry>`

          `<mesh>`

            `<uri>model://custom_map/meshes/your_model.obj</uri>`

          `</mesh>`

        `</geometry>`

      `</visual>`

    `</link>`

  `</model>`

`</sdf>`

* `<static>true</static>` ensures the map remains fixed.

---

### **4\. Load the Map in Gazebo**

1. Open Gazebo and go to **Insert \> Models**.  
2. Find **CustomMap** and drag it into the simulation.

Alternatively, launch it using:  
bash  
CopyEdit  
`gz sim --verbose`
